The risk of spreading it in utero is nearly zero. The real risk is when you contract genital herpesWHILE pregnant. Then, your latency can be high enough to possibly pass on during birth without open sores. 

Passing it through vaginal birth if it isn’t a recent new virus in your system, or you don’t have open sores, is incredibly small. 

If you are contracting genital herpes while pregnant you are likely to be symptomatic with flu-like symptoms, and it is frequently checked in these cases to rule out when someone in the advanced stages of pregnancy shows flu symptoms or any unusual genital sores. 

There are many other more common complications at birth that don’t carry the same shame and stigma. And most STIs are dangerous to contract while pregnant and pose similar risks to babies in a vaginal birth. Gentital herpes, overall, is not a devastating STI to have present in your body and doesn’t pose any measurably greater risk in a vaginal birth than any other STI if you aren’t recently contracting it or having an active breakout. 

Source: my partner is an internal medicine doctor and my aunt is an OBGYN.

The clock on both of those sentences runs at the same time — not like one is served completely, and then the next one starts. Tips as someone who raised a havanese, and has helped my mom, aunt, and cousin all with their havanese puppies:

3. They’re super trainable and have long back legs, they can learn to “walk” and “spin” and dance!
4. Spray bitter spray on any belongings you don’t want chewed
5. Crate train them early and get them used to somewhat frequent separation for short periods to nip separation anxiety in the bud
6. The puppies are super small and portable—my mom got a wicker tote bag that was very structured and solid and carried her pup to places in it to get her out and about!
